statedGuarantee: An AARM-conformant runtime security system intercepts every AI-driven action before it reaches a tool, accumulates session context (original user request, prior actions, data classifications accessed), evaluates the action against both static policy and contextual intent alignment, synchronously enforces one of five authorization decisions (ALLOW/DENY/MODIFY/STEP_UP/DEFER) such that denied and deferred actions produce no effects on target systems, binds each action to human/service/agent identity, and emits a cryptographically signed, offline-verifiable tamper-evident receipt. The distinctive claim beyond ordinary policy enforcement is context-aware PREVENTION: blocking compositions (e.g. read customer PII, then send external email) that no single action reveals in isolation, plus detection of intent drift via semantic distance from the original request.
advertisedRhetoric: The paper advertises enforcement strength per-architecture rather than for the specification as a whole. Protocol Gateway: “Enforcement point: Network level. If network configuration ensures all tool traffic routes through the gateway, enforcement cannot be bypassed by agent-side code.” Kernel/eBPF: “Enforcement point: Kernel level. All system calls from the agent process pass through eBPF hooks. User-space code cannot bypass kernel enforcement without kernel compromise.” and “Bypass risk: Lowest of any architecture. Evasion requires kernel-level exploit or running outside the monitored environment.” SDK Instrumentation, candidly: “Bypass risk: Higher than gateway architecture. Malicious code, bugs, or misconfiguration could invoke tools directly without passing through AARM.” Globally the spec calls the action layer a “natural chokepoint for policy enforcement” and mandates that “No effects MUST occur on target systems for denied or deferred actions” and that “The system MUST NOT have a fail-open mode that bypasses policy evaluation.”
tierSpan: Not covered: Direct HTTP calls bypassing the protocol, raw database connections, local filesystem access, shell command execution, or tools using non-standard protocols. || Kernel-level (eBPF/LSM) implementations alone cannot satisfy AARM conformance for context-dependent allow, deny, or defer classifications. These classifications require semantic understanding of actions and accumulated session context—information that is fundamentally unavailable at the syscall level. || eBPF implementations SHOULD therefore be positioned as defense-in-depth backstop layers alongside semantic-aware enforcement architectures (Gateway, SDK, or Vendor Integration) that provide the context-dependent evaluation required for full AARM conformance. Vendors must not claim AARM compliance based solely on kernel-level monitoring. || [SDK] Bypass risk: Higher than gateway architecture. Malicious code, bugs, or misconfiguration could invoke tools directly without passing through AARM.
cheapestDefeat: Perform the effect through any path that does not traverse the mediation chokepoint. Worked explicitly: (1) GUARANTEE - no action reaches a tool without synchronous policy evaluation, and denied/deferred actions produce no effects. (2) MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL - the interposition point, which in every architecture capable of satisfying conformance is an application-layer chokepoint: an MCP/protocol proxy the agent is configured to dial (Gateway), an in-process callback/middleware hook the agent framework is configured to call (SDK), or a vendor-side pre-execution hook inside the vendor's own runtime (Vendor Integration). (3) CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION - issue a raw HTTP request, open a direct database connection, write the local filesystem, or exec a shell command instead of invoking a registered tool. No exploit, no signature forgery and no kernel compromise is required; the paper enumerates each of these paths itself as uncovered. A subprocess or an FFI call that never enters the instrumented code path achieves the same thing. (4) TIER OF THE MECHANISM DEFEATED - T3, an application proxy / chokepoint. WHY NOT T2: the only OS-tier mechanism offered, eBPF/LSM, is disqualified by the specification's own conformance clause from carrying the guarantee alone and is prescribed as a backstop that can enforce only the FORBIDDEN class via static IP/path/syscall rules - not AARM's distinctive claim. A layered Gateway+eBPF deployment raises the floor to T2 only for that static subset, while the context-dependent classes stay pinned at T3. WHY NOT T1: receipts really are signed (Ed25519 / ECDSA P-256 / RSA-2048) and offline-verifiable, which is genuine T1 for the audit record, but signatures bind only what a verifier accepts about records that were produced. An actor that routes around the mediator generates no receipt at all, so the cryptography never binds the effector - the same structure as the worked example in which an in-process hook makes signature forgery unnecessary.
placementSpan: Agents process untrusted data from multiple channels, any of which may contain adversarial content [ 7 ] : • User inputs: Direct prompt injection attacks embedded in user messages [ 18 ] . • Retrieved documents: Indirect injection via RAG pipelines, where malicious instructions are embedded in documents the agent retrieves and processes [ 7 ] . • Tool outputs: Adversarial content returned by compromised or malicious tools, interpreted by the agent as instructions rather than data. || The AI model and orchestration layer cannot be trusted as a security boundary. Security controls that depend on the model “doing the right thing” will fail when the model is manipulated, confused, or simply wrong. || Untrusted: – The AI model and its outputs – The orchestration layer (agent framework, workflow logic) – User inputs and prompts – Tool outputs and retrieved data – External documents, emails, and web content – Agent memory and conversation history || Trusted: – The AARM system (action mediation, context accumulator, policy engine, receipt generator) – Cryptographic primitives and key management – The policy store and policy authoring process – The underlying infrastructure (OS, network, hardware)

coverageSpans.E1: [Gateway] Not covered: Direct HTTP calls bypassing the protocol, raw database connections, local filesystem access, shell command execution, or tools using non-standard protocols. || [SDK] Not covered: Tools invoked through uninstrumented paths, native code called via FFI, or tools added after initial instrumentation. || Coverage completeness depends on integration thoroughness. Partial instrumentation creates gaps that sophisticated attacks may exploit.
coverageSpans.E2: [SDK] Covered: All tools invoked through instrumented code paths, including HTTP clients, database drivers, filesystem APIs, shell execution, and custom integrations. || [SDK] Not covered: Tools invoked through uninstrumented paths, native code called via FFI, or tools added after initial instrumentation. || [Gateway] Not covered: Direct HTTP calls bypassing the protocol, raw database connections, local filesystem access, shell command execution, or tools using non-standard protocols. || [eBPF] Covered: All syscalls from monitored processes: network I/O, filesystem access, process creation. [Nothing in the spec re-mediates the actions a spawned descendant subsequently takes; the eBPF line scopes to 'monitored processes' without addressing descendant inclusion, and eBPF alone is non-conformant.]
coverageSpans.E3: Sensitive data may leak through channels outside the primary action path: verbose log outputs, debug traces, error messages with stack traces containing data fragments, or metadata in external API calls. These leakage vectors bypass action-level policy enforcement because the data exfiltration occurs as a side effect of permitted operations rather than through explicit tool invocations. || Comprehensive side-channel prevention requires complementary controls at the infrastructure level. || [eBPF] Limited visibility: Encrypted network payloads (TLS) cannot be inspected without additional decryption. || [Gateway] Not covered: Direct HTTP calls bypassing the protocol, raw database connections, local filesystem access, shell command execution, or tools using non-standard protocols.
coverageSpans.E4: An action a a is a discrete operation the agent requests against a tool. || t is the target tool (e.g., email , database , slack ) || [SDK] Covered: All tools invoked through instrumented code paths, including HTTP clients, database drivers, filesystem APIs, shell execution, and custom integrations. [VCS/git push is never named anywhere in the paper; coverage is inherited only from this generic tool-agnostic action model, and only for paths actually instrumented or routed.]
coverageSpans.E5: [SDK] Covered: All tools invoked through instrumented code paths, including HTTP clients, database drivers, filesystem APIs, shell execution, and custom integrations. || [Gateway] Not covered: Direct HTTP calls bypassing the protocol, raw database connections, local filesystem access, shell command execution, or tools using non-standard protocols. || Model training data poisoning or weight manipulation: Pre-deployment threats requiring ML security, model provenance, and supply chain controls. [Package install, install hooks, and their network activity are never addressed; only a top-level install invocation on an instrumented shell path would be seen as an action.]
coverageSpans.E6: The system SHOULD support credential scoping for minimal permissions per action. • Just-in-time credential issuance with minimal validity period • Operation-specific scoping (e.g., read-only for query operations) • Credential usage logged for audit || Privilege amplification. Autonomous agents routinely operate under static, high-privilege identities that are misaligned with the principle of least privilege || Even perfect contextual prevention fails if the agent’s execution identity is too powerful, a core mismatch with zero-trust principles. [No credential list is published anywhere in the specification, and R9 is a SHOULD, not a MUST.]
coverageSpans.E7: In multi-agent architectures, a compromised or manipulated agent may delegate tasks to other agents, propagating malicious intent across trust boundaries. || AARM Partial Mitigation: Cross-agent context tracking preserves the chain of intent across agent boundaries, enabling downstream agents to evaluate actions against the original user request rather than only the delegating agent’s instructions. ... Full mitigation requires distributed tracing standards and federated receipt verification that remain under active research. || As agents delegate to other agents, action chains become distributed across multiple orchestration contexts. Maintaining coherent authorization and audit trails across agent boundaries is unsolved.

schneider.surrogate: A per-action execution monitor: synchronous pre-execution interception of each tool invocation (R1); evaluation of the action tuple (tool, operation, parameters, identity) against static policy plus a predicate over an append-only hash-chained session-context log (R2/R3); a five-valued decision with DENY-on-timeout defaults and bounded cascading deferral (R4); identity binding validated for freshness and revocation (R6); and a signed receipt per decision (R5). Each of these is a safety property - decided on a finite prefix of the action trace and, once violated, violated irrevocably - so an execution monitor sitting at the action boundary can enforce it. R7's semantic-distance threshold is likewise a monitorable predicate over the prefix.
schneider.objective: Prevention of compositional information flow - that no sequence of individually-permitted actions ever effects exfiltration, and that actions remain aligned with the user's true intent. Exfiltration-by-composition is an information-flow property over the data rather than a property of any single trace, hence a hyperproperty outside the enforceable class; 'intent alignment' compounds this because intent is a latent, unobservable predicate over an opaque reasoning process. The paper effectively concedes both: the reasoning process “is not inspectable or verifiable. We observe inputs and outputs but cannot reliably determine ‘intent’”, and the objective is filed under open research - “Can we build reliable intent classifiers, or must we accept that some attacks will be semantically indistinguishable from legitimate operations?” and “How do we track data lineage through non-deterministic transformations?” The abstract nevertheless advertises the objective (“evaluates against policy and intent alignment”), which is precisely the split.

notes:
WHY THE DEPLOYMENT-DEPENDENT TIER DOES NOT ACTUALLY SPLIT. This paper was flagged as a test of whether the rule handles a document that names kernel eBPF as one implementation among several, and so might score T2 or T3 by deployment choice. It does not split, and the reason is in the paper itself rather than in the coding rule: Section VI-C-4 (Conformance Limitation) disqualifies eBPF-only deployments from claiming conformance at all - 'Vendors must not claim AARM compliance based solely on kernel-level monitoring' - and Table IV encodes this in the row 'AARM-conformant alone: Gateway Yes / SDK Yes / eBPF No* / Vendor If hooks sufficient'. Every conformant deployment therefore contains a T3 semantic-aware chokepoint (Gateway, SDK, or Vendor hook), and weakest-link scoring lands on T3 in all four deployment shapes. What the eBPF layer genuinely buys is a T2 floor for the FORBIDDEN class only (static rules on IPs, file paths, syscalls); the three context-dependent classes that constitute AARM's novelty are, by the paper's own analysis, unreachable at the syscall layer ('Context access: None'). A coder tempted to score this T2 on the strength of 'Bypass resistance: Very High' in Table IV would be scoring an advertised property of a configuration the specification itself declares non-conformant. Recommend the SoK record this as the clean case where a paper's own conformance clause, not the adjudicator, resolves the tier.

NO IMPLEMENTATION, NO EVALUATION - EVIDENCE IS L0. This is a specification document; there is no artifact, no code, no measurement, and no adversarial testing anywhere in it. The author states the intent plainly: 'The goal is not to build AARM, but to define what an AARM system must do.' Each conformance requirement carries a prescriptive 'Verification:' paragraph telling a future implementer what to test, but none of those tests were run by the author. Consequently the ADVERSARY PLACEMENT field is unusual: the instruction asks for the placement 'the evaluation actually tests', and here the evaluation tests nothing. I coded A2 as primary because the entire threat model and every worked example is built on adversarial content arriving through inputs and retrieved context (direct and indirect prompt injection, malicious tool outputs, memory poisoning, environmental manipulation), and coded A3/A4/A1 as secondary because the design addresses them without testing: A3 through 'intent drift', which the paper is careful to distinguish from adversarial injection ('whether the agent was manipulated by an attacker or simply drifted through its own reasoning'); A4 because treating the orchestration layer as potentially compromised is the paper's founding premise; A1 as the generic external attacker behind injection. A5 is NOT coded even as secondary - the trust assumptions place 'The underlying infrastructure (OS, network, hardware)' and the AARM system itself in the TRUSTED column, and 'Physical or infrastructure-level attacks' in Out of Scope. An adjudicator who believes flagging an addressed-but-untested placement requires an artifact should downgrade the secondaries; I kept them because the instruction explicitly allows placements 'the design addresses but does not test'.

WHY EVERY EFFECTOR IS PARTIAL AND NONE IS 'COVERED'. Three independent reasons stack, any one of which alone would cap the whole row. (1) The chokepoint is architectural, so the DEPTH RULE bites everywhere: nothing in the specification mediates a spawned descendant's own actions, its egress, or an install hook's network activity. The action model is defined over invocations the agent 'requests against a tool'; a child process is not an agent action-request and is never brought back under mediation. (2) The COVERT-CHANNEL RULE bites E3 directly and honestly: Section V-C-3 concedes that leakage via logs, debug traces, stack-trace fragments and 'metadata in external API calls' bypasses action-level enforcement 'because the data exfiltration occurs as a side effect of permitted operations rather than through explicit tool invocations'. That candor is admirable and does not close the gap. (3) Every architecture publishes its own not-covered list. This all-partial row is not a criticism disguised as a score - it is what a spec governing a declared-tool boundary can honestly claim, and this paper is more forthcoming about its gaps than most in the corpus.

THE TWO SOFT CELLS AN ADJUDICATOR SHOULD RE-READ. E4 (VCS push) and E5 (package install) are the weakest calls in this coding and I flag them rather than bury them. Neither effector is named anywhere in the paper - there is no mention of git, VCS, npm, pip, or install hooks. Read strictly, the rule 'a system that simply does not address an effector scores not-covered' would push both to not-covered. I scored them partial instead because the action model is deliberately tool-agnostic - an action is (tool, operation, parameters, identity, context, timestamp) over an open tool set - and the SDK architecture explicitly lists 'shell execution' among covered code paths, so a git push or an npm install issued through an instrumented path genuinely is intercepted, which is a real reach and not an arguable one. What is provably NOT reached in either case: the same commands issued through an uninstrumented path or a subprocess, and for E5 the third-party install hooks and their network activity, which execute below the action layer entirely and are never contemplated. If the adjudicator prefers a strict named-effector reading, flipping E4 and E5 to not-covered is defensible and would not disturb the tier, the placement, or the Schneider verdict.

E6 IS CAPPED TWICE - BY AN UNDEFINED LIST AND BY A 'SHOULD'. First, the depth rule: there is no published credential list anywhere in the specification, so partial is the ceiling by construction. Second, and worth noting for the SoK's treatment of MUST-versus-SHOULD, least-privilege enforcement is R9, an Extended (SHOULD) requirement that 'may be omitted with documented justification' - so an 'AARM Core' compliant system can satisfy every MUST requirement while doing nothing at all about credential scoping. R6 (identity binding) is a MUST, but it binds identity TO actions for attribution; it does not mediate a read of an env var, a config file, a keychain, or a cloud metadata endpoint. The paper diagnoses this effector well ('Even perfect contextual prevention fails if the agent's execution identity is too powerful') and then addresses it only at SHOULD strength.

ONE PLACE THE PAPER IS STRONGER THAN ITS TIER. The receipt requirement (R5) is real cryptography - Ed25519 / ECDSA P-256 / RSA-2048 minimum, canonical serialization, public keys published for offline verification - and R2 recommends an append-only hash-chained context log. For the AUDIT property (a receipt cannot be retroactively altered undetected) that is genuinely T1. It does not lift the enforcement tier, because an action routed around the mediator produces no receipt to tamper with; the crypto binds records, not effectors. Worth recording separately if the SoK ever splits enforcement tier from evidentiary tier.
